\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
The central finding of our experiments is that restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
ESS-only reweighting (which maximizes $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$) yields PPL 17.737, worse than the uniform baseline (17.694, Table~\ref{tab:main}).
The dual-constrained adaptive $\bstar$, by contrast, achieves 17.651 by selecting the \emph{smallest} $b$ that meets the quality floor $\tau$.
The mechanism is clear from the binding statistics: in the 38.2\% of reweighted batches where $\aeff$ binds, the dual-constrained $\bstar$ (median 0.80, mean 1.19) is far below the ESS-only upper bound (median 3.59, mean 5.88), a 4.9$\times$ over-intervention ratio (mean); the $\aeff$ constraint prevents substantial over-intervention.
This binding rate is consistent across contamination levels (38.2\% at $\rho{=}0.4$ vs.\ 33.4\% at $\rho{=}0.6$, a gap ${<}5$ percentage points), and the $\bstar$ distribution differs by ${<}2\%$ in coefficient of variation across seeds, so the dual constraint adapts its behavior proportionally rather than requiring per-$\rho$ reconfiguration.
This proportion-robust behavior has a structural explanation: ESS binding dominates (${\sim}$61--66\% of batches across $\rho \in \{0.4, 0.6\}$), and the ESS constraint is by construction independent of the population contamination rate; it depends only on within-batch weight concentration.
Over-downweighting discards gradient signal from borderline samples whose detector scores are intermediate (e.g., $q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$); these samples carry partial but non-negligible training value, and aggressively suppressing them impoverishes the effective training distribution.
The $\aeff$ constraint prevents this by halting $b$ as soon as the quality target is met.

\paragraph{$\tau$ as a practical dial.}
The quality threshold $\tau$ controls the trade-off between decontamination strength and sample retention.
Our sweep (Table~\ref{tab:tau}) reveals a wide safe operating range: all $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ outperform uniform training, with PPL varying only 0.035 across this interval.
The sensitivity is asymmetric: under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) incurs mild degradation ($-$0.006 to $-$0.015 vs.\ uniform), while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bar{b}^* = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$, 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$).
This asymmetry reinforces the minimum intervention intuition: the cost of doing too little is small, whereas the cost of doing too much is steep.
Across tested contamination levels, $\tau \in [0.7, 0.8]$ is optimal (Appendix~\ref{app:tau_rho}): $\tau{=}0.8$ at $\rho{=}0.4$ and $\tau{=}0.7$ at $\rho{=}0.6$.
We recommend $\tau = 0.8$ as a principled default for moderate contamination; practitioners can adjust within the safe range $[0.5, 0.8]$ with low risk, or follow the heuristic $\tau \approx 1 - \rho/2$ when a rough contamination estimate is available.
